overview.text: Emmanuel Macron is a French politician who was first elected president in May 2017 and reelected in April 2022. Before the presidency, he served as deputy secretary-general in the president’s office and then as minister for the economy, industry, and digital affairs. In 2016 he founded En Marche!, a political movement that provided the platform for his first presidential campaign. France’s president is elected by direct vote for a five-year term and appoints a prime minister. He had founded En Marche! only a year before winning his first presidential election. His second term began with an inauguration in May 2022.

key_facts.text: Macron founded En Marche! on 6 April 2016.
He won his first presidential election on 7 May 2017.
He was reelected on 24 April 2022.
He served as economy minister from 2014 to 2016.
The French president appoints the prime minister.

overview.text: William Wallace was a Scottish knight and resistance leader during the First War of Scottish Independence. After Edward I of England invaded Scotland, Wallace joined a wider uprising in 1297. He and Andrew Moray led Scottish forces to victory at Stirling Bridge in September of that year. Wallace became a Guardian of Scotland, acting on behalf of the deposed King John Balliol. Edward I defeated his army at Falkirk in July 1298, after which Wallace resigned the guardianship but continued to resist English rule. Captured in 1305, he was taken to London and executed. Records of his early life are sparse, so later legends should be separated from these documented events.

Wallace was appointed a Guardian of Scotland after Stirling Bridge.
Edward I defeated Wallace’s forces at Falkirk in July 1298.

overview.text: Benjamin Netanyahu is an Israeli politician associated with the Likud party and several long periods as prime minister. He first took office after the 1996 election, served again from 2009 to 2021, and returned after the 2022 election. His long tenure makes the changes between election, coalition formation, and governing important parts of his political story. Before becoming prime minister, he also held foreign-affairs and finance posts. In 2019 Israel’s attorney general announced corruption charges against him in three cases, including a bribery charge in one case. Those are allegations in a criminal proceeding, not a finding of guilt. Netanyahu’s career is tied to debates over Israeli coalition politics and the accountability of leaders.

He served continuously as prime minister from 2009 to 2021.
He returned to the premiership after the 2022 election.
Netanyahu has been a leader of the Likud party.

overview.text: Ancient Rome was a civilization that grew from a city on the Italian peninsula into a power spanning much of the Mediterranean world. Its political history included kings, a republic, and rule by emperors. During the republic, aristocratic patricians initially held many privileges, while poorer citizens pressed for representation and land. Expansion through conquest and diplomacy brought wealth but also inequality and civil conflict. After the assassination of Julius Caesar, Octavian emerged dominant and received the title Augustus in 27 BCE. Roman rule continued in western and eastern regions for centuries, while its provinces developed diverse local cultures, cities, and trade networks. Its political institutions and material remains are major sources for studying antiquity.

key_facts.text: Rome became a republic around 509 BCE.
Republican expansion relied on conquest and diplomacy.
Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE.
Octavian received the title Augustus in 27 BCE.

overview.text: Howard Carter was a British archaeologist whose team uncovered the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. Excavations began in November, and a step found on 4 November led to a sealed entrance. Carter peered into the tomb’s antechamber on 26 November, revealing furnishings and other objects. Lord Carnarvon financed the search; Egyptian workers and a wider group of specialists took part in excavation, documentation, conservation, and removal. The burial chamber was opened in February 1923, and systematic clearance continued for years. Carter’s detailed records now help researchers study the tomb’s objects and the process by which they were recovered.

key_facts.text: Carter’s team found a stairway to the tomb on 4 November 1922.
He looked into the antechamber on 26 November 1922.
Lord Carnarvon funded Carter’s search.
The burial chamber was opened in February 1923.
The tomb’s clearance and documentation took about a decade.
Egyptian workers played a vital role in uncovering and clearing the tomb.

overview.text: The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was an agreement signed by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union on 23 August 1939. Its public terms promised that the two states would not attack each other. A secret protocol assigned parts of eastern Europe to German or Soviet spheres of influence and planned a division of Poland. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Soviet forces entered from the east on 17 September. The pact gave both governments room for territorial expansion, despite their sharply opposed ideologies. It did not create a lasting peace: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, ending the agreement. The pact’s secret terms are central to understanding Poland’s wartime partition.

key_facts.text: The agreement was signed on 23 August 1939.
Its public terms pledged nonaggression.
A secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence.
Germany and the Soviet Union both invaded Poland in September 1939.
Germany broke the pact by invading the Soviet Union in June 1941.

overview.text: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon in the eighteenth century BCE whose rule is remembered for both political power and a famous inscribed collection of judgments. The surviving monument, now in the Louvre, is a tall dark stone stela carved around 1750 BCE. Its relief shows the king before Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun god associated with justice. Below are 282 judgments addressing matters such as family, property, trade, and labor. They describe how a ruler presented and applied justice, though the text is not a modern code of law. One provision about injury illustrates the principle of proportionate retaliation often summarized as “an eye for an eye.”

key_facts.text: Hammurabi ruled Babylon in the eighteenth century BCE.
The surviving stela contains 282 legal judgments.
Its upper relief shows Hammurabi before Shamash.
The judgments address family, property, trade, and labor.
The stela was discovered at Susa in 1902.

overview.text: The Thermidorian Reaction began with the fall of Maximilien Robespierre and his allies during the French Revolution. On 9 Thermidor Year II in the revolutionary calendar, or 27 July 1794, opponents in the National Convention moved against Robespierre and Saint-Just. They were arrested; Robespierre and other supporters were executed the next day. Their fall ended the dominance of the radical Montagnard leadership and the phase known as the Terror. The reaction was also a longer political turn against institutions and practices associated with that period, not merely a single execution. Opponents of Robespierre combined fear of political purges with rejection of the Terror’s excesses.

The National Convention moved against Robespierre and Saint-Just.
Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794.
The events ended the Montagnard Convention and the Terror.

overview.text: The Marshall Plan, formally the European Recovery Program, was a United States aid effort to help Europe recover after World War II. Secretary of State George C. Marshall proposed a broad recovery program in a Harvard speech on 5 June 1947. Congress authorized funding in 1948, and the program supported reconstruction and renewed industrial activity in Western Europe. American officials also feared that severe economic hardship would strengthen communist movements during the emerging Cold War. The plan brought investment to European industry and became a significant form of U.S. foreign aid. Its name honors Marshall, but the program required congressional approval and cooperation among multiple governments.

Congress authorized the program in 1948.
It was formally called the European Recovery Program.
The program helped Western European reconstruction after World War II.
Cold War concerns were among the reasons U.S. leaders backed it.

overview.text: Hadrian ruled the Roman Empire from 117 to 138 CE after the emperor Trajan. He traveled through the empire and emphasized the defense and organization of existing frontiers. During his visit to Britain in 122, he ordered construction of the wall that bears his name along the northern frontier of the Roman province of Britannia. Soldiers built the fortification; it was not the modern border between England and Scotland. Hadrian’s reign also included the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judaea, fought from 132 to 135 and suppressed by Roman forces. That conflict brought severe harm to Jewish communities. These events show both the reach of Roman administration and the violence that could accompany imperial rule.

He succeeded Trajan.
Construction of Hadrian’s Wall began in 122 CE.
The wall marked the northern frontier of Roman Britannia.
The Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–135 was suppressed under Hadrian.
